extrapolated_to_target_usable.method: mean pages per usable user times the target

edge_list.note: the live run kept only the first parent per user, which is a spanning tree; a tree is acyclic by construction, so it cannot answer whether the pool is one clique. This is the graph.

notes: Step 4 forecast, aggregated over the 4088 usable users confirmed so far: 210500 calls, 23.39 hours at the 150/min throttle. Mean 51.49 pages per user, median 36, p95 151, max 1034. The top decile of users holds 0.3516 of the pages.

The forecast the live run stored was wrong, not merely un-summed: it divided `total_plays`, which is absent from 77 percent of users/:id/stats payloads, so most users forecast exactly one page. It is now computed from episodes.plays + movies.plays, which is always present and which equals total_plays wherever total_plays exists.

Plateau rule state: moving average 3.877 against a peak of 12.333, ratio 0.314 against a trigger of 0.2. The closest the run has come is a ratio of 0.193. The rule has not fired and no threshold in it has been changed.

Rounds whose clock looks like a stall rather than throttling: [8]. A stall is one enormous gap between consecutive requests with no 429 in the round; throttling is many small gaps. The live run recorded only a single wall-clock number, in which the two are identical.

Throttle sleep per round was never recorded by the client and is not derivable from the request log, so it is null with source not_recoverable. It has not been estimated. The largest inter-request gap is measured and answers what throttle sleep was wanted for.
